sentence: Where the oceanic Nazca Plate descends beneath the South American Plate, the downgoing slab dehydrates at depths approaching one hundred kilometres. Released fluids lower the melting point of the overlying mantle wedge, generating arc magmas that ascend to feed the Andean volcanic chain. The slab's negative buoyancy drives much of the convergence.

Slab rollback occurs when a descending lithospheric plate sinks faster than the trench advances, causing the trench to migrate oceanward. This extension thins the overriding plate and opens back-arc basins. The phenomenon explains the curvature of many island arcs and the episodic spreading recorded in their marginal seas.

Beneath the Tohoku margin, the seismogenic zone extends from roughly fifteen to forty kilometres depth, bounded updip by unconsolidated sediment and downdip by the brittle-ductile transition. Coseismic slip in the 2011 rupture propagated unexpectedly far updip, reaching the trench and generating an exceptionally large tsunami.

Flat-slab subduction develops where buoyant features such as oceanic plateaus or aseismic ridges resist sinking. The shallowly inclined slab scrapes along the base of the continent, shutting off the asthenospheric wedge and suppressing arc volcanism while broadening the zone of crustal deformation far inland.

The Benioff zone is delineated by earthquakes that track the descending slab to depths near seven hundred kilometres. Below that, the slab either stalls at the mantle transition or penetrates into the lower mantle, depending on the local thermal structure and the resistance offered by the six-hundred-sixty-kilometre discontinuity.

Accretionary prisms grow as offscraped trench sediment is stacked into imbricate thrust sheets at the toe of the overriding plate. Each new thrust slice underplates beneath older material, and the wedge maintains a critical taper governed by the balance between basal friction and internal strength.

Episodic tremor and slip events on the Cascadia interface release strain quietly over weeks, accompanied by faint non-volcanic tremor. These slow slip episodes recur roughly every fourteen months and load the locked seismogenic patch updip, incrementally raising the probability of a great megathrust rupture.

When two oceanic plates converge, the older and colder one usually sinks because its greater density provides the driving slab pull. The resulting intra-oceanic arc, such as the Marianas, is built almost entirely of mantle-derived magma with little continental contamination.

Forearc basins accumulate sediment in the topographic low between the trench and the volcanic arc. Their stratigraphy records the tectonic history of the margin, preserving unconformities tied to subduction erosion, accretion, and changes in the dip of the underlying slab.

Subduction erosion removes material from the base of the overriding plate, tectonically thinning the continental margin over millions of years. Evidence comes from the landward migration of the volcanic front and from arc basement rocks now exposed unexpectedly close to the trench.

The silica tetrahedron, a single silicon atom coordinated by four oxygens, is the fundamental building block of the silicate minerals. The degree to which these tetrahedra polymerise, sharing corner oxygens, defines the structural classes from isolated nesosilicates to fully linked tectosilicates.

Olivine is a nesosilicate in which independent tetrahedra are bound together by divalent cations occupying octahedral sites. Iron and magnesium substitute freely across the forsterite-fayalite series, and the resulting solid solution controls the mineral's density, melting behaviour, and refractive properties.

In the pyroxenes, tetrahedra share two corners to form single chains running parallel to the c-axis. The chains are bonded laterally by cations in two distinct sites, M1 and M2, whose differing sizes accommodate cations from calcium down to aluminium.

Amphiboles extend the chain motif into double chains, creating ribbons with a characteristic hexagonal cavity that hosts hydroxyl groups and large cations. The presence of structural water distinguishes amphiboles from the otherwise similar pyroxenes and lowers their thermal stability.

Sheet silicates form when three of the four tetrahedral oxygens are shared, producing infinite two-dimensional layers. Micas, clays, and chlorite all share this architecture, and their perfect basal cleavage reflects the weak bonding between adjacent silicate sheets.

Quartz represents the fully polymerised endmember in which every tetrahedral oxygen is shared with a neighbour, yielding a continuous three-dimensional framework of composition silicon dioxide. The framework's helical arrangement of tetrahedra gives quartz its piezoelectric behaviour and optical handedness.

Feldspars are framework silicates in which aluminium substitutes for some silicon, and the resulting charge deficit is balanced by potassium, sodium, or calcium in large cavities. Coupled substitution governs the alkali and plagioclase solid solution series.

The garnet group adopts an isometric structure with isolated tetrahedra linked through eight-coordinated and six-coordinated cation sites. Wide cation substitution produces a continuum from pyrope to almandine to grossular, each variety carrying information about the pressure and temperature of its formation.

Zeolites are framework silicates whose open architecture encloses channels wide enough to admit water molecules and exchangeable cations. The reversible uptake and loss of these guest species without collapse of the aluminosilicate scaffold underlies their use as molecular sieves.

Aluminium plays a dual role in silicate minerals, occupying tetrahedral sites in substitution for silicon and octahedral sites alongside magnesium and iron. The partitioning of aluminium between these coordinations is sensitive to pressure and serves as a geobarometer in metamorphic assemblages.

A depositional sequence is bounded by unconformities and their correlative conformities, recording one full cycle of relative sea-level change. Within each sequence the systems tracts stack in a predictable order, allowing the prediction of facies away from well control.

During a relative fall in sea level, the shoreline steps basinward and rivers incise into the exposed shelf. The resulting sequence boundary is a surface of subaerial exposure and erosion, commonly mantled by a lag of coarse, reworked sediment.

The transgressive systems tract is deposited as accommodation outpaces sediment supply, driving a landward shift of facies. Its base is the transgressive surface, and parasequences within it stack retrogradationally, each one stepping further landward than the last.

The maximum flooding surface marks the turnaround from transgression to regression, often expressed as a condensed section of slowly accumulated, fossil-rich sediment. On wireline logs it frequently appears as a sharp gamma-ray peak rich in radioactive clay.

Highstand deposits accumulate when sediment supply finally exceeds the creation of accommodation, producing a progradational, basinward-building wedge. These clinoforms downlap onto the maximum flooding surface and record the gradual filling of the available space.

A parasequence is the fundamental stratal unit, a relatively conformable succession of beds bounded by marine flooding surfaces. Each parasequence typically coarsens upward as the shoreline progrades, then is abruptly capped by deeper-water facies at the flooding event.

The falling-stage systems tract comprises sediment deposited during forced regression, when the shoreline is driven seaward by a falling base level. Its detached, downstepping shoreface sandbodies form important stratigraphic traps for hydrocarbons.

Accommodation, the space available for sediment to accumulate, is governed by the combined effects of eustasy and tectonic subsidence. Sequence stratigraphy interprets stratal geometries as the sedimentary response to changing rates of accommodation and supply.

Onlap, downlap, and toplap are the diagnostic reflection terminations seen on seismic sections. Mapping these relationships allows the recognition of sequence boundaries and systems tracts even where the rocks themselves are never sampled by drilling.

Carbonate sequences differ from siliciclastic ones because the sediment is generated in place by organisms whose productivity depends on water depth and light. A rapid relative rise can drown a carbonate platform outright if production cannot keep pace with the rising sea.

A meandering river migrates laterally as the outer, concave bank erodes and a point bar accretes on the inner bank. Over time the channel sweeps across its floodplain, leaving a record of scroll bars and abandoned oxbow lakes that mark former positions.

Braided rivers carry coarse bedload across low-gradient reaches where the discharge is highly variable. The channel splits around mid-channel bars of gravel and sand, and the whole network reorganises during each flood as bars are dissected and rebuilt.

A river's longitudinal profile is typically concave upward, steep in the headwaters and gentle near the mouth. The graded profile represents a balance in which the channel's slope is just sufficient to transport the sediment supplied to it.

Knickpoints are abrupt steepenings in a river's long profile, often marking the upstream limit of a wave of incision triggered by base-level fall. As the knickpoint retreats headward it lowers the channel and rejuvenates the surrounding landscape.

Alluvial fans build where a confined mountain stream debouches onto a basin floor and abruptly loses its capacity to carry sediment. The flow spreads, deposits its coarsest load near the apex, and the channel periodically switches position to construct a radial cone.

River terraces are abandoned floodplain surfaces left perched above the modern channel after a phase of incision. Paired terraces flanking a valley at the same elevation record a former equilibrium level subsequently disrupted by uplift or climate change.

The competence of a stream is the largest particle it can move, while its capacity is the total sediment load it can carry. Both rise sharply with discharge, so most geomorphic work in a river is accomplished during infrequent flood events.

Drainage networks evolve toward characteristic patterns dictated by the underlying geology. Dendritic networks develop on uniform substrate, trellis patterns reflect alternating resistant and weak strata, and radial drainage spreads outward from a structural or volcanic dome.

During a flood the river overtops its banks and deposits the suspended fines across the floodplain. The coarsest of this overbank sediment settles closest to the channel, building natural levees that stand slightly above the surrounding backswamp.

Stream capture occurs when the headward erosion of one drainage breaches the divide and diverts the flow of a neighbouring catchment. The beheaded stream is left underfit, occupying a valley far too large for its diminished discharge.

As a basaltic magma cools, minerals crystallise in the order predicted by Bowen's reaction series, with high-temperature olivine and calcic plagioclase appearing first. Their removal progressively enriches the residual liquid in silica, alkalis, and water.

Fractional crystallisation drives a magma toward more evolved compositions when early-formed crystals are physically separated from the liquid. Dense ferromagnesian minerals settle through the chamber, leaving a residual melt depleted in iron and magnesium.

Crystal mush models picture a magma chamber as a crystal-rich framework permeated by interstitial melt. Differentiated liquids are extracted by compaction and filter pressing, ascending to form the evolved cap that erupts during the most explosive episodes.

Magma mixing produces hybrid rocks with disequilibrium textures: resorbed crystals, reverse zoning, and mafic enclaves quenched against a cooler felsic host. The streaky banding records the incomplete blending of two magmas of contrasting composition.

Assimilation of country rock changes a magma's chemistry as wallrock is melted and incorporated. Combined with simultaneous fractional crystallisation, this process leaves distinctive isotopic fingerprints that betray a crustal contribution to the ascending melt.

Layered mafic intrusions such as the Bushveld Complex display rhythmic layering in which successive bands are enriched in different cumulus minerals. The layering records repeated episodes of crystal accumulation on the floor of a slowly cooling chamber.

Liquid immiscibility splits a single melt into two coexisting liquids of contrasting composition, one rich in silica and one rich in iron. Globular textures preserved in some basalts and ferrobasalts record this unmixing during the late stages of solidification.

The Daly gap describes the relative scarcity of intermediate compositions in many volcanic suites. It is attributed to the rapid crossing of the intermediate field during fractional crystallisation, so that erupted magmas are predominantly mafic or felsic.

Partial melting of the mantle produces basaltic magma whose composition depends on the degree of melting and the depth at which melt segregates. Small degrees of melting at depth yield alkaline magmas, while larger degrees at shallower levels yield tholeiites.

Volatile saturation occurs when a rising magma can no longer hold its dissolved water and carbon dioxide. The exsolving bubbles expand explosively as confining pressure drops, driving the fragmentation that powers a Plinian eruption column.

The uranium-lead method exploits two independent decay chains, allowing a sample to be dated twice from the same mineral. When the two ages agree the result is termed concordant, providing a powerful internal check on the integrity of the system.

Zircon is the workhorse mineral of high-precision geochronology because it incorporates uranium during crystallisation but excludes lead. Its robust crystal lattice resists later disturbance, so the trapped daughter product faithfully records the time of growth.

Discordant uranium-lead analyses plot below the concordia curve when a mineral has lost some of its radiogenic lead. The intercepts of a best-fit discordia line constrain both the original crystallisation age and the time of the disturbing event.

The potassium-argon clock starts when a mineral cools below the temperature at which argon ceases to escape. Because the daughter is a gas, the method dates cooling rather than crystallisation and is sensitive to later reheating.

Argon-argon dating refines the older potassium-argon technique by measuring isotopes of a single element on an irradiated sample. Step-heating releases gas from different lattice sites, and a flat age spectrum signals an undisturbed sample.

An isochron is constructed by plotting the daughter isotope against the parent, both normalised to a stable reference isotope. The slope of the line yields the age, and the intercept reveals the initial isotopic composition of the system.

Radiocarbon dating measures the decay of an unstable carbon isotope produced in the upper atmosphere. With a half-life near fifty-seven hundred years, the method is restricted to organic material younger than roughly fifty thousand years.

Closure temperature is the temperature below which a mineral retains its radiogenic daughter product. Different minerals close at different temperatures, so dating several phases from one rock reconstructs a continuous cooling history.

The samarium-neodymium system is valued for its resistance to disturbance by metamorphism and weathering. Because both elements are immobile rare earths, the method dates ancient events that have erased more fragile chronometers.

Detrital zircon populations carry the age fingerprint of the source terranes that shed them. Dating hundreds of grains from a sandstone yields a spectrum of ages that constrains provenance and the timing of basin filling.

A normal fault accommodates extension as the hanging wall slips downward relative to the footwall along a surface that typically dips between sixty and seventy degrees. Repeated movement drops elongate blocks to form the grabens characteristic of rift settings.

Reverse faults shorten the crust by driving the hanging wall up and over the footwall. When the fault plane dips gently, at less than thirty degrees, the structure is termed a thrust and may transport rock for tens of kilometres.

Strike-slip faults accommodate horizontal motion with little vertical displacement. Along releasing bends the crust pulls apart to form transtensional basins, while restraining bends squeeze the rock upward into pop-up structures and flower geometries.

Fault gouge is the finely comminuted rock produced by grinding within a fault zone. Its clay-rich, low-permeability character can seal a fault, while the surrounding fractured damage zone may instead act as a conduit for migrating fluids.

Slickensides are the polished, striated surfaces left where two blocks have slid past one another. The orientation of the striations records the direction of the most recent slip, and asymmetric steps reveal its sense.

Listric faults flatten with depth, curving from a steep dip near the surface into a near-horizontal detachment. The hanging wall must deform internally to remain in contact with the curved surface, producing a rollover anticline.

A fault scarp is the topographic step left at the surface by a dip-slip earthquake. Its initially sharp free face degrades over time as the slope retreats and a wedge of colluvium accumulates at its base.

The frictional behaviour of a fault is described by rate-and-state laws that determine whether slip is stable or seismic. Velocity-weakening surfaces can nucleate earthquakes, whereas velocity-strengthening material tends to creep aseismically.

Fault-bend folds form where a thrust sheet is forced to climb a ramp connecting two flat detachments. The hanging wall must bend to negotiate the change in fault dip, generating a fold whose geometry can be predicted from the ramp angle.

Transfer faults link offset segments of a normal fault system, accommodating differences in extension between adjacent blocks. They allow strain to be partitioned along strike without requiring the displacement on any single fault to be continuous.

A turbidity current is a dense, sediment-laden flow that races down the continental slope and spreads across the basin floor. Each pulse deposits a graded bed, coarse at the base and fining upward, recording the waning of the current.

Aeolian dune deposits are recognised by their large-scale cross-bedding, excellent sorting, and frosted, well-rounded grains. The steep foreset laminae dip downwind, preserving the migration of the dune across an ancient desert floor.

In a tidal flat, sediment is sorted across the intertidal zone, with sand near the low-water line grading landward into mud. Alternating sand and mud laminae, deposited on successive tides, build the rhythmically banded tidal bedding.

Deltaic deposits form where a river loses energy on entering a standing body of water. The classic delta builds a topset, foreset, and bottomset succession, recording the progradation of the river mouth into deeper water.

Carbonate reefs are built by framework organisms that secrete calcium carbonate skeletons in warm, shallow, clear water. The rigid reef framework, its talus apron, and the lagoon behind it together form a distinctive set of facies.

Glacial till is an unsorted, unstratified mixture of clay, sand, and boulders dumped directly from melting ice. Its chaotic texture and faceted, striated clasts distinguish it from the sorted sediment laid down by meltwater streams.

An evaporite sequence records the progressive concentration of a restricted water body. As evaporation proceeds, minerals precipitate in order of increasing solubility, from carbonate through gypsum to halite and finally the bitter potash salts.

Submarine fans accumulate at the mouths of canyons that funnel sediment from the shelf to the deep basin. Leveed channels feed lobes of sand at the fan's edge, building a cone of turbidites that can host substantial petroleum reservoirs.

Estuarine sediments record the mixing of fresh and marine waters in a drowned river valley. The interplay of fluvial supply, tidal currents, and wave action sorts the deposits into a tripartite arrangement that shifts as relative sea level changes.

Lacustrine deposits laid down in a deep, stratified lake are often finely laminated, recording the seasonal cycle of sedimentation. Pairs of light and dark laminae, termed varves, allow the annual counting of the lake's depositional history.

The geologic timescale divides Earth's history into a nested hierarchy of eons, eras, periods, and epochs. Each boundary is fixed by a globally agreed reference section, a point in a rock succession chosen to anchor the division worldwide.

The Precambrian, spanning the Hadean, Archean, and Proterozoic eons, accounts for nearly nine tenths of Earth's history. Its sparse and cryptic fossil record long resisted subdivision, so its boundaries are defined chronometrically rather than by biological events.

The Phanerozoic Eon begins with the appearance of abundant, shelly fossils and is divided into the Palaeozoic, Mesozoic, and Cenozoic eras. The era boundaries coincide with major mass extinctions that reorganised the biosphere.

The Cambrian Period records an explosive diversification of animal body plans within a few tens of millions of years. The base of the Cambrian, and of the Phanerozoic itself, is defined by the first appearance of a distinctive trace fossil.

A golden spike, formally a Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point, physically marks the base of a chronostratigraphic unit in a chosen outcrop. The marker fixes the definition of the boundary against which all other sections are correlated.

The Quaternary Period encompasses the repeated glacial cycles of the past two and a half million years. It is subdivided into the Pleistocene, dominated by ice ages, and the comparatively brief and warm Holocene.

Biostratigraphy correlates rocks by their contained fossils, using rapidly evolving and widely distributed species as index forms. The first and last appearances of these species furnish the datums that subdivide the geologic record.

The Anthropocene has been proposed as a new unit recognising the planetary scale of human influence on sediments, climate, and biota. Debate centres on whether a single, globally synchronous marker can be identified to define its base.

Numerical ages calibrate the relative timescale by attaching dates in years to its boundaries. Radiometric dating of volcanic ash beds interbedded with fossiliferous strata ties the biostratigraphic framework to absolute time.

The Proterozoic witnessed the rise of atmospheric oxygen, the assembly and breakup of supercontinents, and severe global glaciations. Its subdivision into eras and periods relies on these large-scale chemical and tectonic events rather than on fossils.

Hawaiian eruptions are the gentlest style, characterised by the effusive outpouring of fluid basaltic lava. Low gas content and low viscosity allow the magma to flow freely, building broad shield volcanoes with gentle slopes.

Strombolian activity consists of rhythmic, mildly explosive bursts as large gas bubbles rise through a magma column and burst at the surface. Each explosion ejects incandescent clots of lava that accumulate into a steep-sided cinder cone.

Vulcanian eruptions are short, violent blasts that clear a vent plugged by viscous, degassed magma. The explosions fragment the plug and any older rock, hurling dense blocks and ash in cannon-like discharges.

Plinian eruptions sustain a towering column of gas and ash that can pierce the stratosphere. Driven by the rapid exsolution of volatiles from silica-rich magma, they blanket vast areas in pumice and ash fall.

A pyroclastic flow is a ground-hugging avalanche of hot gas, ash, and rock fragments that descends a volcano's flanks at lethal speed. It forms when an eruption column collapses or a lava dome fails catastrophically.

Phreatomagmatic eruptions are powered by the explosive interaction of magma with external water. The flash conversion of water to steam shatters the magma into fine ash, producing wide, low-rimmed craters called maars.
Lava domes grow by the slow extrusion of magma too viscous to flow far from the vent. Their steep, unstable flanks shed rockfalls and, on collapse, can spawn devastating pyroclastic flows.

Flood basalt eruptions emplace immense volumes of fluid lava from fissures over geologically brief intervals. The resulting layered plateaus, such as the Deccan Traps, coincide with episodes of severe environmental stress.

A lahar is a fast-moving slurry of volcanic debris and water that pours down river valleys draining a volcano. It can be triggered by the melting of summit ice, intense rainfall, or the breaching of a crater lake.

The explosivity of an eruption is gauged by the Volcanic Explosivity Index, a logarithmic scale based on erupted volume and column height. Each step represents a roughly tenfold increase in the magnitude of the event.

The greenschist facies represents low-grade metamorphism, where chlorite, actinolite, and albite give mafic rocks their characteristic green hue. The mineral assemblage records temperatures around three to five hundred degrees at modest depth in the crust.

Amphibolite facies conditions convert a basalt into a rock dominated by hornblende and plagioclase. The disappearance of chlorite and the growth of aluminous garnet mark the transition from the underlying greenschist field.

Granulite facies metamorphism occurs at the highest crustal temperatures, where hydrous minerals break down and pyroxene replaces hornblende. The resulting rocks are dry, coarse-grained, and record conditions deep in a thickened orogen.

The blueschist facies forms only along the cool, high-pressure path of a subduction zone. Sodic amphibole and lawsonite are diagnostic, and their preservation requires rapid exhumation before the rock warms and the minerals revert.

Eclogite is the high-pressure equivalent of basalt, composed of green omphacitic pyroxene and red pyrope-rich garnet. Its dense assemblage forms where oceanic crust is dragged to mantle depths within a descending slab.

Contact metamorphism produces the hornfels facies in a narrow aureole around an igneous intrusion. The heat recrystallises the country rock into a tough, fine-grained, non-foliated rock whose mineralogy maps the thermal gradient.

A facies series traces the pressure-temperature path followed by a region during an orogeny. The Barrovian series records moderate geothermal gradients, while the Buchan series reflects the higher gradients of shallower, hotter terranes.

Index minerals appear at specific grades, and the surfaces in the field that mark their first appearance are isograds. Mapping the chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, and sillimanite isograds reveals the thermal architecture of a metamorphic belt.

Prograde metamorphism proceeds as temperature rises, driving devolatilisation reactions that release water and carbon dioxide. The escaping fluids carry heat and dissolved species, and their loss tends to make later retrograde reactions sluggish.

The aluminosilicate triple point, where kyanite, andalusite, and sillimanite coexist, anchors metamorphic phase diagrams. Which polymorph a rock contains is a sensitive guide to the pressure and temperature it experienced.

An aquifer is a body of rock or sediment porous and permeable enough to yield usable quantities of water. A confined aquifer is bounded above and below by impermeable units, so its water is held under pressure greater than atmospheric.

The water table is the surface below which the pores of the rock are fully saturated. It is not flat but a subdued replica of the overlying topography, rising beneath hills and intersecting the ground at springs and streams.

Darcy's law relates the rate of groundwater flow to the hydraulic gradient and the permeability of the medium. Water moves from areas of high hydraulic head to low, and the discharge is proportional to the steepness of that gradient.

An artesian well taps a confined aquifer in which the pressure is sufficient to drive water above the top of the aquifer. Where the potentiometric surface lies above the ground, the water flows freely without pumping.

A cone of depression develops around a pumping well as the water table is drawn down. If pumping outpaces recharge, the cone widens and deepens, lowering water levels and potentially capturing flow from neighbouring wells.

The recharge zone is the area where surface water infiltrates to replenish an aquifer. Rainfall, snowmelt, and streamflow percolate through the unsaturated zone, and the balance of recharge against discharge governs the long-term yield.

Porosity measures the fraction of a rock occupied by void space, while permeability measures how easily fluid passes through those connected voids. A clay can be highly porous yet nearly impermeable because its pores are minute and poorly linked.

A perched aquifer forms where a lens of impermeable clay holds a body of groundwater above the regional water table. Springs issuing from a hillside often mark the edge of such a perched, locally saturated zone.

Saltwater intrusion threatens coastal aquifers when excessive pumping lowers the freshwater head. Dense seawater advances inland along a wedge beneath the lighter fresh water, contaminating wells near the coast.

Groundwater residence times range from days in shallow flow paths to many millennia in deep regional systems. Isotopic tracers and dissolved gases allow hydrogeologists to estimate how long water has been isolated from the atmosphere.

Porphyry copper deposits form above a cooling intrusion where hot, metal-bearing fluids fracture the rock and precipitate sulphide minerals in a dense network of veinlets. These low-grade but enormous orebodies supply much of the world's copper.

Volcanogenic massive sulphide deposits accumulate on the seafloor where hydrothermal vents discharge metal-laden fluids. The metals precipitate as the hot fluid mixes with cold seawater, building mounds of copper, zinc, and lead sulphides.

Banded iron formations are chemical sediments laid down in the Precambrian ocean, recording alternating layers of iron oxide and chert. They are the chief source of iron ore and a record of the early oxygenation of seawater.

Placer deposits concentrate dense, durable minerals such as gold and cassiterite where flowing water sorts sediment by density. The heavy grains lag behind in riffles and the inner bends of channels while lighter material is swept away.

Skarn deposits develop where a hot intrusion reacts with adjacent carbonate rock, producing calc-silicate minerals and concentrating metals. The chemical contrast between magma and limestone drives the fluids that deposit the ore.

Mississippi Valley-type deposits host lead and zinc sulphides in carbonate rocks far from any igneous body. The metals were carried by warm basinal brines that migrated through the strata and precipitated their load in porous zones.

Lateritic deposits form by intense tropical weathering, which leaches soluble elements and leaves an insoluble residue. Nickel, aluminium, and iron are concentrated near the surface as the rock decomposes under prolonged warm, wet conditions.

An epithermal gold deposit forms at shallow depth from hot, near-surface fluids associated with volcanism. Gold is deposited in veins and breccias as the fluids boil, cool, and mix with descending meteoric water.

Magmatic sulphide deposits form when an immiscible sulphide liquid separates from a mafic magma and scavenges nickel, copper, and platinum. The dense sulphide droplets settle and pool at the base of the intrusion.

A pegmatite is an exceptionally coarse-grained igneous rock crystallised from a water-rich residual melt. The late fluids concentrate rare elements such as lithium, beryllium, and tantalum into giant, well-formed crystals.

Trace fossils record the behaviour of ancient organisms rather than their bodies, preserving burrows, trackways, and feeding marks. Because they cannot be transported far from where they were made, they faithfully indicate the original environment.

Ichnofacies group trace fossils into recurring assemblages tied to particular settings. The Skolithos ichnofacies of vertical dwelling burrows marks high-energy sandy shorelines, while the Cruziana assemblage indicates quieter, deeper water.

Bioturbation is the disruption of primary sedimentary layering by burrowing and grazing organisms. Intense bioturbation can destroy bedding entirely, leaving a thoroughly churned, mottled fabric that signals slow deposition and an oxygenated bottom.

Dinosaur trackways preserve the size, gait, and speed of their makers. The spacing of consecutive footprints, combined with leg length estimated from track dimensions, allows the walking velocity of an extinct animal to be reconstructed.

Coprolites are fossilised faeces whose contents reveal the diet of long-dead animals. Bone fragments, scales, and plant tissue trapped within them link a predator or herbivore to the organisms it consumed.

The trace fossil Zoophycos forms a spreite of stacked, sweeping laminae produced by a deposit feeder systematically mining the sediment. Its distinctive geometry records an efficient strategy for processing nutrient-poor mud.

Stromatolites are layered structures built by communities of microbes that trap and bind sediment. Among the oldest evidence of life, they record the activity of microbial mats stretching back more than three billion years.

Borings differ from burrows in that they are excavated into a hard substrate such as rock, shell, or wood. Organisms that bore for shelter leave clean-walled cavities that cut sharply across the grains of the host material.

The first appearance of complex, branching burrows near the base of the Cambrian marks a profound change in animal behaviour. The deepening and intensification of bioturbation transformed the chemistry of the seafloor sediment.

Escape traces record an animal's struggle to keep pace with rapid sedimentation. A series of stacked, upward-arching laminae shows where a buried organism repeatedly tunnelled upward to maintain contact with the sediment surface.

An earthquake radiates two kinds of body waves through the Earth's interior. Primary waves compress and dilate the rock in their direction of travel, while slower secondary waves shear it at right angles to their path.

Secondary waves cannot pass through a liquid because fluids have no resistance to shear. The absence of these waves on the far side of the Earth from a quake is the principal evidence that the outer core is molten.

Seismic waves bend, or refract, as they cross boundaries where wave speed changes. The systematic curvature of ray paths through the mantle reveals the increase of velocity with depth and the position of major discontinuities.

Surface waves travel along the Earth's outer skin and carry most of the destructive energy of a large earthquake. Love waves shake the ground horizontally, while Rayleigh waves roll it in a retrograde elliptical motion.
The shadow zone is a band on the globe where direct primary waves fail to arrive because the liquid core refracts them sharply. Its angular width furnishes a precise measure of the core's radius.

Seismic tomography assembles travel-time data from many earthquakes and stations into a three-dimensional image of the Earth's interior. Slow regions are interpreted as warm, buoyant mantle and fast regions as cold, descending slabs.

The Mohorovicic discontinuity, marked by an abrupt jump in seismic velocity, defines the base of the crust. Its depth varies from a few kilometres beneath the oceans to tens of kilometres beneath mountain belts.

The travel-time difference between the first primary and secondary arrivals widens with distance from the source. Measuring this interval at a single station yields the distance to the earthquake, and three stations fix its location.

Wave amplitude is strongly affected by the material it traverses. Soft, water-saturated sediment amplifies ground motion and prolongs shaking, which is why basins underlain by loose fill suffer disproportionate earthquake damage.

The inner core, although under immense pressure, transmits a faint shear wave, indicating that it is solid. Its solidity arises because the freezing point of iron rises with pressure faster than the temperature does at that depth.

Frost wedging shatters rock as water repeatedly freezes and expands within cracks. The roughly nine percent volume increase on freezing exerts enormous pressure, prising joints apart and reducing exposed bedrock to angular rubble.

Chemical weathering attacks rock through reactions with water and atmospheric gases. Hydrolysis converts feldspar into clay minerals, while the dissolution of carbonate by weak carbonic acid sculpts the landscapes of limestone terrains.

Spheroidal weathering rounds initially angular blocks as chemical alteration penetrates inward from joint surfaces. Corners are attacked from three sides at once, so they decay fastest, leaving a core of fresh rock wrapped in concentric shells of decomposed material.

Exfoliation strips curved sheets from a rock mass as confining pressure is released by the erosion of overlying material. The unloaded rock expands and fractures parallel to the surface, producing the smooth domes of granite landscapes.

Salt weathering disintegrates porous rock as crystals grow within its pores. The pressure exerted by the growing crystals, fed by repeated cycles of solution and evaporation, hollows out the cavities seen in desert sandstone.

Oxidation rusts the iron-bearing minerals of a rock, staining it in shades of red and brown. The conversion of iron to its oxidised state weakens the crystal lattice and prepares the mineral for further breakdown.
Biological weathering combines mechanical and chemical attack by living organisms. Roots prise rock apart as they thicken, and lichens secrete acids that etch the mineral surface to which they cling.

The rate of weathering depends on climate, rock type, and the duration of exposure. Warm, humid conditions accelerate chemical decay, whereas cold, dry climates favour the slower mechanical breakdown of fresh rock.

A weathering rind is the discoloured, softened outer layer that develops on a clast over time. Because the rind thickens at a roughly predictable rate, its thickness can be used to estimate how long a surface has been exposed.

Differential weathering exploits contrasts in rock resistance, leaving hard layers standing in relief while weak layers are etched back. The resulting ledges, recesses, and hoodoos express the underlying variation in mineralogy and cementation.

A glacier behaves as a slowly flowing solid, moving by internal deformation of ice crystals and by sliding over its bed. Where meltwater lubricates the base, the whole mass can surge forward at greatly accelerated rates.

Glacial erosion operates by plucking and abrasion. The ice freezes onto and quarries blocks from the bedrock, then drags the entrained debris across the surface, grinding it smooth and scoring it with parallel striations.

A cirque is an amphitheatre-shaped hollow excavated at the head of a glacial valley. Repeated freezing, plucking, and rotational flow steepen its headwall and deepen its floor, often leaving a small lake when the ice retreats.

Glacial valleys are carved into a broad parabolic cross-section, in contrast to the V-shape of river valleys. Tributary glaciers fail to cut as deeply as the trunk, so on deglaciation their valleys are left hanging high above the main floor.

A moraine is a ridge of unsorted debris deposited by a glacier. Lateral moraines build along the ice margins, a medial moraine forms where two glaciers merge, and a terminal moraine marks the furthest advance of the ice.

Drumlins are streamlined hills of glacial till sculpted beneath moving ice. Their elongate, asymmetric form, blunt up-ice and tapered down-ice, records the direction in which the overriding glacier flowed.

Eskers are sinuous ridges of sand and gravel deposited by meltwater streams flowing through tunnels within or beneath a glacier. When the ice melts away, the channel fill is left as a winding embankment across the landscape.
An erratic is a boulder transported by ice and deposited far from its bedrock source. Tracing an erratic back to its origin reveals the direction and extent of former glacial transport.

Outwash plains spread beyond a glacier's margin as braided meltwater streams sort and deposit sediment. The deposits fine away from the ice, grading from coarse gravel near the front to sand and silt downstream.

Isostatic rebound lifts land that was depressed beneath the weight of a former ice sheet. Long after the ice has gone, the crust continues to rise slowly as the underlying mantle flows back into the unloaded region.

Mid-ocean ridges are the longest mountain chains on Earth, marking the divergent boundaries where new oceanic crust is created. Magma rises into the rift, freezes onto the plate edges, and is carried away symmetrically on both sides.

Abyssal plains are the flattest surfaces on the planet, blanketing the deep ocean floor with a smooth layer of fine sediment. Pelagic clay and the rain of microscopic skeletons accumulate slowly over the rugged volcanic basement.

Seamounts are submarine volcanoes that rise steeply from the deep-sea floor. Many were once active above sea level, and a flat-topped guyot records a former island whose summit was planed off by waves before it subsided.

Magnetic stripes on the seafloor record reversals of the Earth's field as crust forms and cools at a ridge. The symmetrical pattern of normal and reversed bands on either side confirmed the hypothesis of seafloor spreading.

Hydrothermal vents discharge superheated, mineral-rich fluid where seawater circulates through hot crust near a spreading centre. Precipitating sulphides build chimneys, and the chemical energy sustains an ecosystem independent of sunlight.

The continental shelf is the shallow, gently sloping submerged margin of a continent. Beyond its edge the gradient steepens at the continental slope, which descends to the deep ocean floor across the more gradual rise.
Submarine canyons incise the continental slope, channelling sediment from the shelf to the deep sea. They are kept open by turbidity currents that periodically scour their floors and walls.

Ocean drilling recovers cores of sediment and basement rock that archive the history of the ocean basins. The succession of microfossils and the magnetisation of the basalt date the crust and reconstruct past climate.

Passive continental margins, lacking a plate boundary, accumulate thick sedimentary wedges as the adjacent ocean widens. They subside steadily as the underlying crust cools and the load of sediment depresses it further.

Manganese nodules grow on the abyssal floor at extraordinarily slow rates, accreting metal oxides over millions of years. Their concentric internal layering preserves a record of changing deep-ocean chemistry.

A soil profile is organised into horizons that develop as weathering and biological activity alter the parent material downward. The uppermost horizons are enriched in organic matter, while deeper ones grade into unaltered rock or sediment.

The five soil-forming factors are parent material, climate, organisms, topography, and time. Their interplay determines whether a given site develops a thin, immature soil or a deep, strongly differentiated one.

Leaching strips soluble and fine material from the upper horizons and carries it downward. The depleted zone of removal is the eluvial horizon, and the underlying zone where the washed-down material accumulates is the illuvial horizon.

Laterite forms under intense tropical weathering, where prolonged leaching removes silica and bases and leaves a residue of iron and aluminium oxides. The resulting soil is brick-red, nutrient-poor, and hardens irreversibly on drying.

Caliche is a hardened layer of calcium carbonate that accumulates in the soils of arid regions. Carbonate dissolved in infiltrating water precipitates at the depth to which moisture typically penetrates, cementing the soil into a resistant crust.

A podzol develops under cool, wet conditions on sandy parent material. Organic acids strip iron and aluminium from a bleached, ash-grey upper horizon and redeposit them in a dark, rust-coloured horizon below.
Soil texture is defined by the proportions of sand, silt, and clay. The texture governs how readily water drains, how much moisture the soil retains, and how easily plant roots penetrate it.

A paleosol is an ancient soil buried and preserved within a sedimentary succession. Its horizons and chemistry record the climate and surface conditions that prevailed during a long pause in deposition.

Soil structure refers to the way individual particles bind into aggregates called peds. Well-developed crumb or blocky structure creates the pore network that admits air and water and supports a healthy root zone.
Vertisols are clay-rich soils that swell when wet and shrink when dry. The repeated volume changes open deep cracks, churn the profile, and heave the surface into a hummocky microrelief.

The mantle, extending from the base of the crust to the core, comprises the bulk of the Earth's volume. Although solid, it deforms slowly over geological time, convecting heat from the deep interior toward the surface.
The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell that includes the crust and the uppermost mantle. It rests on the weaker, partially yielding asthenosphere, over which the lithospheric plates glide.

The mantle transition zone, between roughly four hundred and six hundred sixty kilometres depth, is marked by mineral phase changes. Olivine transforms to denser structures, and these abrupt density jumps reflect seismic waves.

Mantle convection is driven by the contrast between hot, buoyant material rising from depth and cold, dense slabs sinking from the surface. This slow overturn is the engine that ultimately drives plate motion.

Mantle plumes are columns of unusually hot rock that ascend from deep within the mantle, possibly from the boundary with the core. Where a plume head reaches the lithosphere it can generate a long-lived volcanic hotspot.

The core-mantle boundary is the sharpest internal discontinuity in the planet, separating the silicate mantle from the iron-rich liquid outer core. The thin layer just above it shows anomalous seismic properties and may be partially molten.

The outer core is a churning shell of molten iron and nickel whose convective motion generates the Earth's magnetic field. The field is sustained by a self-exciting dynamo powered by the heat escaping from the inner core.

Geothermal heat flows outward from the interior, supplied by the decay of radioactive isotopes and by the slow cooling of the core. The gradient measured in mines and boreholes reflects this steady loss of internal energy.

Hotspot volcanism builds chains of islands as a plate drifts over a stationary deep-mantle source. The age of each volcano increases away from the active centre, recording both the direction and the rate of plate motion.

Seismic anisotropy, the variation of wave speed with direction, reveals the alignment of mantle minerals by flow. Mapping it constrains the pattern of convection in the otherwise inaccessible interior.

Karst terrain develops where soluble carbonate bedrock is dissolved by slightly acidic water. Surface drainage vanishes underground through swallow holes, and the resulting landscape is pocked with closed depressions and laced with caves.

A sinkhole forms when the roof of a dissolved cavity collapses or when surface material slumps into a void below. Cover-collapse sinkholes can appear suddenly, swallowing roads and buildings as the supporting soil gives way.

Speleothems decorate cave interiors as carbonate precipitates from dripping water. Stalactites grow downward from the ceiling and stalagmites build upward from the floor, occasionally meeting to form a continuous column.

A polje is a large, flat-floored depression in karst country, often bounded by steep walls. Its floor is sealed with impermeable sediment and may flood seasonally when the underground drainage cannot carry the water away fast enough.

Cave passages develop along the joints and bedding planes that guide the flow of groundwater. The geometry of a cave system therefore mirrors the structural fabric of the rock through which it has been dissolved.

Tower karst consists of steep, isolated residual hills rising abruptly from a flat alluvial plain. The towers are remnants of a once-continuous limestone mass, left standing as the surrounding rock was progressively dissolved away.

A karst spring discharges water that has travelled through a network of dissolved conduits. Such springs respond rapidly to rainfall and often carry sediment, betraying the fast, turbulent, pipe-like flow of the underground system.

Lapies, or limestone pavement, is a fretted bedrock surface dissected by solution-widened joints. The bare blocks between the fissures are sculpted into runnels and pits where rainwater has etched the exposed rock.

Pseudokarst landscapes mimic the closed depressions and caves of true karst but form in insoluble rock by other processes. Lava tubes, piping in loose sediment, and the melting of buried ice all produce karst-like features.

The vadose zone above the water table hosts caves that are still forming, with passages cut by free-flowing streams. Below the water table, in the phreatic zone, dissolution proceeds in fully water-filled tubes of more rounded cross-section.

An earthquake occurs when accumulated elastic strain is released suddenly along a fault. The rock on either side springs back toward its unstrained shape, and the stored energy radiates outward as seismic waves.

The focus, or hypocentre, is the point at depth where rupture begins, and the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it. Most damaging continental earthquakes nucleate in the upper twenty kilometres of the crust.

The moment magnitude scale measures an earthquake's size from the rigidity of the rock, the fault area that slipped, and the average displacement. Unlike older scales, it does not saturate for the very largest events.

Aftershocks follow a large earthquake as the crust adjusts to the redistributed stress. Their frequency decays in a predictable way, falling off roughly in inverse proportion to the time elapsed since the main shock.

Liquefaction occurs when strong shaking causes a water-saturated sandy soil to lose its strength and behave as a fluid. Buildings tilt and sink, and buried tanks float upward, as the ground momentarily loses its bearing capacity.

The elastic rebound theory holds that crustal blocks deform slowly under tectonic stress until a fault breaks. The two sides snap past one another, the strain is released, and the cycle of slow loading begins again.

Intensity describes the strength of shaking and the damage experienced at a particular place, and so varies across the affected region. Magnitude, by contrast, is a single number quantifying the total energy released at the source.

A tsunami is generated when an undersea earthquake abruptly displaces a column of water. The disturbance spreads as long-wavelength waves that travel fast in deep water and rear up to great height as they reach shallow coasts.

Seismic hazard maps express the probability that ground shaking of a given severity will be exceeded at a site within a stated period. They synthesise the locations of faults, their slip rates, and the attenuation of waves with distance.

The focal mechanism of an earthquake, the so-called beachball, depicts the orientation of the fault and the direction of slip. It is derived from the pattern of compressions and dilations recorded at seismometers around the globe.

A petroleum system requires a source rock, a reservoir, a seal, and a trap, all assembled in the correct sequence. The failure of any one element prevents the accumulation of a producible deposit of oil or gas.

Source rocks are organic-rich mudstones in which the remains of plankton and algae are buried and preserved. With burial and heating the organic matter is converted into hydrocarbons that can later migrate away.

The oil window is the range of temperature, roughly sixty to one hundred twenty degrees, over which a source rock generates liquid petroleum. At higher temperatures the system enters the gas window and yields predominantly methane.

Migration carries hydrocarbons from the source rock into a porous reservoir. Buoyant oil and gas rise through the pore network until they are halted beneath an impermeable seal, accumulating in the structurally highest position.

An anticlinal trap holds hydrocarbons in the arched crest of a fold, where an impermeable caprock prevents their further ascent. Gas collects at the top, oil beneath it, and water occupies the pores below the oil.

Stratigraphic traps depend on lateral changes in the rock rather than on folding or faulting. A reservoir sandstone that pinches out updip into impermeable shale can hold a substantial accumulation without any structural closure.

Reservoir quality is governed by porosity, which stores the fluid, and permeability, which allows it to flow to a well. Both can be degraded by compaction and by the precipitation of cement in the pore spaces during burial.

Maturity indicators such as vitrinite reflectance gauge how much heat a source rock has experienced. The progressive darkening and ordering of organic particles records the thermal history of the basin.

Unconventional reservoirs hold hydrocarbons in rock too tight to flow naturally. Shale gas and tight oil are produced only after hydraulic fracturing creates an artificial network of permeability connecting the rock to the wellbore.

Basin modelling reconstructs the burial, heating, and migration history of a sedimentary basin through time. By simulating when source rocks matured and traps formed, it assesses whether hydrocarbons could have charged a prospect.

The hardness of a mineral, its resistance to being scratched, is gauged on a comparative scale running from soft talc to diamond. Each mineral on the scale will scratch those below it and be scratched by those above.

Cleavage is the tendency of a mineral to break along planes of structural weakness. The number of cleavage directions and the angles between them reflect the internal bonding and are diagnostic of mineral identity.

Lustre describes how a mineral surface reflects light. The metallic shine of pyrite, the glassy gleam of quartz, and the greasy or pearly appearance of other species each point toward a particular group.

Streak is the colour of a mineral's powder, obtained by drawing the specimen across an unglazed porcelain plate. It is often more reliable than the colour of the bulk specimen, which can be altered by trace impurities.

Specific gravity compares a mineral's density with that of water. Dense minerals such as galena and barite feel conspicuously heavy in the hand, a property useful for distinguishing them from lighter look-alikes.
Fracture describes how a mineral breaks where it lacks cleavage. The smooth, curved conchoidal fracture of quartz, resembling the inside of a shell, is a familiar example used in identification.

Crystal habit is the characteristic external form a mineral tends to display. Pyrite favours cubes, quartz forms hexagonal prisms, and asbestos minerals grow as fibres, each habit reflecting the underlying lattice.

Some minerals respond to special tests. Calcite effervesces in dilute acid, magnetite deflects a compass needle, and fluorite glows under ultraviolet light, giving each a distinctive diagnostic signature.

Tenacity describes how a mineral deforms under stress. Native copper is malleable and can be hammered flat, mica is elastic and springs back when bent, and most silicates are brittle and simply shatter.

Twinning occurs where two crystals of the same mineral grow in a symmetrical, intergrown relationship. Repeated polysynthetic twinning produces the fine parallel striations seen on cleavage surfaces of plagioclase feldspar.

Continental rifting begins as the lithosphere is stretched and thinned, dropping a central block along bounding normal faults. The East African Rift is a classic example of a continent in the early stages of splitting apart.
As a rift matures, the floor subsides below sea level and the ocean enters, as in the Red Sea. With continued spreading the rift evolves into a new ocean basin floored by basaltic crust.

Rift basins accumulate thick wedges of sediment shed from the uplifted, faulted margins. The earliest fill is commonly coarse alluvial fan and lake deposits, recording rapid subsidence in a restricted, fault-bounded depression.
A failed rift, or aulacogen, is an arm of a three-way rift junction that ceased to spread. It survives as a deep, sediment-filled trough projecting into the continent away from the successful ocean.

Rift-related volcanism erupts magma generated as the rising asthenosphere decompresses beneath the thinning lithosphere. Flood basalts and alkaline lavas commonly accompany the earliest stages of continental break-up.

Half-grabens form where extension is accommodated by faulting on one side only. The basin floor tilts toward the master fault, and the asymmetric sedimentary fill thickens markedly toward the bounding fault.

The transition from rifting to drifting marks the moment the continent finally separates and seafloor spreading takes over. The break-up unconformity records this shift from active stretching to thermal subsidence of the new margin.

Mantle upwelling beneath a rift raises the lithosphere into a broad thermal dome before faulting begins. The crest of the dome is stretched, fractured, and ultimately split along the line of the developing rift.

Detachment faults are low-angle structures along which the upper crust slides off the lower during extreme extension. Their footwalls expose deep crustal rocks in the domed culminations known as metamorphic core complexes.

Magma-poor rifted margins expose mantle rock directly on the seafloor where the crust was stretched so severely that it broke before significant melting occurred. Serpentinised peridotite floors the ocean-continent transition.

A geological map portrays the distribution of rock units at the surface, projected as if the soil and vegetation were stripped away. Colours and symbols convey the age, lithology, and structural attitude of each unit.

Strike and dip describe the orientation of a planar feature such as a bedding surface. The strike is the compass direction of a horizontal line on the plane, and the dip is the angle and direction of its steepest descent.

Where a tilted bed crosses a valley, its outcrop trace bends in a characteristic pattern. The rule of Vs states that an inclined contact points upstream in the direction it dips, a relationship used to read structure from a map.

A cross-section is a vertical slice through the map that depicts how units extend into the subsurface. Constructing one forces the geologist to reconcile surface observations into a coherent three-dimensional interpretation.

Contacts between rock units are classified by origin. A depositional contact records sedimentation, an intrusive contact records the emplacement of magma, and a fault contact records the displacement of one block past another.

Field notebooks record the location, lithology, structural measurements, and sketches gathered at each outcrop. This primary documentation is the raw evidence from which the finished map and its interpretation are built.

Stereographic projection plots the orientation of lines and planes onto a circular net. It allows the geologist to manipulate three-dimensional structural data, find intersections, and identify fold axes by graphical means.

Outcrop is the bedrock exposed at the surface, while float is loose, transported rock found nearby. Distinguishing the two is essential, since float can be traced uphill to locate the concealed source outcrop.

Aerial photographs and satellite imagery reveal lineaments, drainage patterns, and tonal contrasts that guide field mapping. Photo interpretation directs the geologist to the key exposures before any ground is walked.

The legend of a geological map arranges the units in stratigraphic order, youngest at the top. It encodes the relative ages and the unconformities that interrupt the succession, summarising the region's geological history.

Rocks preserve a record of past climate in their composition and structure. Coal seams point to ancient swamps, evaporites to arid basins, and tillites to former ice ages, each lithology indexing a particular climatic regime.

The oxygen isotope ratio of marine carbonate records the temperature of the water in which a shell grew and the volume of ice locked on the continents. Measured through a core, it traces the cycle of glacial and interglacial climates.

Glacial striations and dropstones preserved in ancient strata reveal the former presence of ice. Striated pavements beneath Carboniferous tillites mapped the great Gondwanan glaciation across continents now far apart.

Red beds owe their colour to oxidised iron and indicate deposition under a well-aerated, often warm and seasonally dry climate. Their appearance in the rock record tracks the spread of oxidising surface conditions.
Coral growth bands lay down a paired light and dark increment each year, much like tree rings. The spacing of the bands records seasonal cycles and longer fluctuations in sea surface temperature.

Loess is a blanket of wind-blown silt deposited during cold, dry, glacial intervals. Thick loess successions, interrupted by buried soils formed in warmer phases, archive the alternation of glacial and interglacial climate.

Speleothems grow only when water percolates through the rock above a cave, so their layers and chemistry track rainfall. A precisely dated stalagmite can yield a continuous record of past wet and dry periods.

Coal forms where lush vegetation accumulates faster than it decays in waterlogged, oxygen-poor swamps. Extensive coal deposits therefore mark intervals of warm, humid climate and abundant plant growth.

Cyclic sedimentary successions record the rhythmic influence of changes in the Earth's orbit on climate. The regular alternation of facies, tuned to orbital periods, provides a precise astronomical clock for the rock record.

Carbon isotope excursions preserved in marine sediments mark abrupt disturbances of the global carbon cycle. Sharp negative shifts coincide with episodes of rapid warming and the massive release of carbon into the ocean and atmosphere.
A crystal is a solid whose atoms are arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional pattern. The smallest unit that, repeated by translation, builds the entire structure is the unit cell.

Crystals are grouped into seven systems according to the symmetry of their unit cells. The cubic system has the highest symmetry, with three equal, mutually perpendicular axes, while the triclinic system has the lowest.
Symmetry elements describe the operations that leave a crystal's appearance unchanged. Rotation axes, mirror planes, and centres of symmetry combine into the thirty-two distinct crystal classes.
Miller indices label the faces and internal planes of a crystal by their intercepts on the crystallographic axes. The notation provides a compact, universal way to specify any plane in the lattice.

X-ray diffraction probes crystal structure because the regular spacing of atomic planes is comparable to the wavelength of X-rays. The angles at which the beam is diffracted reveal the dimensions of the lattice.

Polymorphs are minerals that share a chemical composition but differ in crystal structure. Diamond and graphite, both pure carbon, owe their utterly different properties to the contrasting arrangement of their atoms.

A solid solution exists where one element substitutes freely for another within a single crystal structure. The olivine and plagioclase series are continuous solid solutions whose composition varies between two endmembers.

Crystal defects, including vacancies, dislocations, and substituted impurity atoms, disturb the otherwise perfect lattice. These imperfections govern how a crystal deforms, conducts, and accommodates trace elements.

Isomorphism occurs when chemically distinct minerals adopt the same crystal structure and form similar crystal shapes. The shared structural template allows them to grow as continuous solid solutions where their cations are interchangeable.

The optical properties of a crystal depend on its symmetry. Cubic minerals are isotropic, transmitting light at one speed in all directions, while lower-symmetry crystals are anisotropic and split light into rays of differing velocity.

Mass wasting is the downslope movement of rock and soil under gravity. It ranges from the imperceptible creep of a hillside to the catastrophic plunge of a rock avalanche, and is a primary agent shaping slopes.

A rotational slump fails along a curved surface, so the displaced mass rotates backward as it slides. The detached block tilts against the slope, leaving a crescent-shaped scarp at its head and a bulging toe below.

A debris flow is a fast, water-saturated slurry of soil, rock, and organic matter that surges down a channel. Capable of carrying boulders, it is among the most destructive of slope failures and can travel far onto valley floors.

Soil creep is the slow, persistent downhill movement of the soil mantle, driven by repeated cycles of wetting, drying, freezing, and thawing. Its effects are seen in tilted poles, bent tree trunks, and bulging walls.

A rockfall occurs where blocks detach from a steep cliff and descend by free fall, bouncing, and rolling. The accumulating debris builds a sloping apron of angular rock, the talus, at the foot of the face.

The factor of safety compares the forces resisting failure with those driving it. When the ratio falls to one, the resisting strength is just balanced by the gravitational stress, and the slope is on the verge of failure.

Pore water pressure is a key control on slope stability, since water in the rock pores reduces the friction along potential failure surfaces. Slopes stable when dry frequently fail during or just after heavy rain.

Solifluction is the slow flow of water-saturated soil over frozen ground in cold climates. The thawed surface layer creeps downslope above the impermeable permafrost, forming distinctive lobes and terraces.

A translational slide moves along a planar surface of weakness, such as a bedding plane or a clay layer parallel to the slope. The displaced sheet of rock or soil slides without the backward rotation seen in a slump.
The angle of repose is the steepest slope that a loose granular material can sustain without sliding. For dry sand it lies near thirty-four degrees, set by the friction between the individual grains.

A geothermal system requires a heat source, a reservoir of permeable rock, and a supply of water. Where all three coincide, circulating fluids extract heat from depth and bring it within reach of the surface.

Hot springs issue where geothermally heated groundwater rises to the surface along faults and fractures. The temperature and chemistry of the water reflect the depth it reached and the rocks through which it passed.

A geyser erupts when water trapped in a constricted underground plumbing system is heated above its surface boiling point. The sudden flashing of the superheated water to steam drives the periodic fountain.
Fumaroles vent steam and volcanic gases where the water table lies too deep for liquid to reach the surface. The escaping vapour deposits sulphur and other minerals around the mouth of the vent.

Geothermal power plants tap reservoirs of hot water or steam to drive turbines. Flash plants exploit high-temperature fluids, while binary plants transfer heat from cooler resources to a low-boiling-point working fluid.

Hydrothermal alteration transforms the rock surrounding a geothermal system as hot fluids react with it. The original minerals are replaced by clays, zeolites, and silica in zones that map the temperature of the circulating water.
Mud pots form where rising steam and gas reach the surface with little water. The vapour mixes with rainwater and altered rock to create a pool of bubbling, acidic mud.

An enhanced geothermal system creates an artificial reservoir by fracturing hot, dry rock and circulating water through it. The technique extends geothermal energy to regions that lack a natural permeable reservoir.

Sinter terraces are deposits of silica laid down by cooling geothermal water. As the hot fluid emerges and loses heat, dissolved silica precipitates, building stepped pools and rims around the discharge.

The geothermal gradient, the rate at which temperature rises with depth, averages around twenty-five degrees per kilometre but is far steeper near volcanic centres. These hot anomalies are the prime targets for geothermal exploration.

Folds form when layered rock is shortened and buckles into a wavy profile. An anticline arches upward with the oldest rocks in its core, while a syncline troughs downward, enclosing the youngest beds at its centre.

The geometry of a fold is described by its hinge, where curvature is greatest, and its limbs, the more planar flanks on either side. The axial surface bisects the fold and connects the hinges of successive layers.

An overturned fold has been tilted so far that one limb is rotated past vertical and the beds within it are upside down. Continued rotation produces a recumbent fold, whose axial surface lies nearly flat.

Cleavage develops in folded rock as platy minerals rotate and grow perpendicular to the direction of greatest shortening. The resulting planar fabric typically fans around the fold, converging toward its hinge.

Ductile deformation allows rock to change shape permanently without fracturing. It dominates at the elevated temperatures and pressures of the deep crust, where rock flows slowly under sustained stress rather than breaking.

Boudinage develops when a competent layer enclosed in weaker rock is stretched. The brittle layer pulls apart into a string of sausage-shaped segments, the boudins, separated by the surrounding rock that has flowed into the gaps.

A foliation is a pervasive planar fabric produced by deformation and metamorphism. Slaty cleavage, schistosity, and gneissic banding represent increasing grades, each recording the alignment of minerals under directed stress.

Strain in a deformed rock can be measured from objects whose original shape is known, such as fossils, ooids, or reduction spots. Their distortion records the magnitude and orientation of the deformation.

Ptygmatic folds are intricately contorted veins within otherwise weakly deformed rock. They form when a thin, competent vein within a flowing matrix is shortened and crumples into tight, irregular puckers.

Mylonite is a strongly foliated rock produced in a ductile shear zone, where intense deformation reduces the grain size. Its fabric records the direction and sense of shear along which the crust slid.

Waves reaching a coast obliquely drive a zigzag transport of sediment along the beach. This longshore drift moves sand steadily in one direction, building spits and starving downdrift shores where it is interrupted.

A sea stack is an isolated pillar of resistant rock left standing offshore as a headland is eroded. It begins as an arch, formed where waves breach a narrow promontory, and becomes a stack when the arch collapses.
A wave-cut platform is a gently sloping bench at the foot of a retreating sea cliff. The platform widens as the cliff is undercut by wave attack and the overhanging rock periodically collapses.

Barrier islands are long ridges of sand separated from the mainland by a lagoon. They migrate landward as storms wash sediment across them, and their evolution is closely tied to changes in sea level.
A tombolo is a ridge of sand or shingle that links an island to the mainland. It forms in the wave shadow behind the island, where reduced energy allows the longshore-transported sediment to settle.

Rip currents are narrow, fast flows that carry water seaward through the surf zone. They develop where water piled against the shore by breaking waves finds a concentrated path back out through the breakers.
Estuaries form where rising sea level drowns the lower course of a river valley. They trap river-borne and marine sediment in a sheltered setting where tidal currents and freshwater flow interact.

A beach profile adjusts to wave conditions, building up under gentle swell and being cut back during storms. Sand removed from the beach face is stored offshore in bars and returned during calmer weather.

Coastal dunes are built where wind transports sand inland from a wide, dry beach. Anchored by vegetation, the dunes form a flexible barrier that absorbs storm energy and exchanges sediment with the beach.

A drowned coastline displays features formed when sea level was lower, now submerged. Rias, the flooded mouths of river valleys, and fjords, the drowned troughs of glacial valleys, both record a relative rise of the sea.

The rock cycle describes the continual transformation of Earth materials among igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic states. Driven by internal heat and surface processes, it recycles the crust over geological time.

The carbon cycle exchanges carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, biosphere, and rocks. Over long intervals the slow burial of carbon in sediment and its release by volcanism and weathering regulate the planet's climate.

Silicate weathering consumes atmospheric carbon dioxide as rainwater dissolves rock and carries the products to the sea. There the elements are locked into carbonate sediment, providing a long-term thermostat for the climate.

Trace elements partition between coexisting minerals and melt according to their compatibility. Compatible elements concentrate in early-formed crystals, while incompatible ones are enriched in the residual liquid.

The rare earth elements behave coherently because of their similar chemistry, so their patterns serve as petrogenetic fingerprints. A depletion of europium, for instance, betrays the earlier removal of feldspar.

Isotopic systems trace the sources and ages of geological materials. The ratios of strontium, neodymium, and lead isotopes distinguish mantle-derived rock from crustal material and track the mixing between reservoirs.

Redox conditions govern the mobility of many elements in surface environments. Iron and manganese dissolve under reducing conditions and precipitate where they encounter oxygen, producing distinctive chemical sediments.

The residence time of an element in the ocean is the average duration it remains dissolved before removal. Reactive elements such as aluminium have short residence times, while conservative ones such as sodium persist for tens of millions of years.

Hydrothermal circulation through oceanic crust modifies seawater chemistry on a global scale. The exchange of elements between hot basalt and circulating water buffers the long-term composition of the ocean.

The sulphur cycle links volcanic emission, the weathering of sulphides, and the burial of sulphur in marine sediment. Bacterial reduction of sulphate to sulphide is a key step that records the oxygenation history of the ocean.

The lunar surface preserves an ancient record because the Moon lacks an atmosphere and active tectonics. Its heavily cratered highlands and smoother volcanic maria have remained largely unchanged for billions of years.

Impact cratering is the dominant geological process on airless bodies. A hypervelocity collision excavates a bowl-shaped cavity, ejects a blanket of debris, and, for larger impacts, leaves a central uplifted peak.

Mars displays the largest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, built by the prolonged eruption of fluid lava onto a stationary crust. The absence of plate motion allowed the shield to grow to immense height.

Channels and valley networks on the surface of Mars record the past flow of liquid water. Their form implies that the early Martian climate was warmer and wetter than the cold, dry conditions of today.

The crater density of a planetary surface measures its age. A heavily cratered terrain has been exposed for a long time, while a sparsely cratered one has been resurfaced more recently by volcanism or other activity.

Tidal heating drives geological activity on some moons of the giant planets. The flexing of Io by Jupiter's gravity makes it the most volcanically active body known, while the same process may keep oceans liquid beneath icy crusts.
Regolith is the layer of fragmented debris produced on an airless world by the relentless bombardment of meteorites. The lunar regolith is a fine, gardened soil churned by countless small impacts.

Differentiation separates a planetary body into a metallic core, a silicate mantle, and a crust. The process is driven by the heat of accretion and radioactive decay, which allows dense material to sink toward the centre.

The Moon is thought to have formed from the debris of a giant impact between the early Earth and a Mars-sized body. The collision ejected molten material that coalesced in orbit to build the satellite.

Cryovolcanism erupts water, ammonia, or methane in place of molten rock on the cold outer worlds. The icy lavas, fluid at the frigid surface temperatures of these bodies, resurface them with smooth, fresh deposits.

Basalt is the most abundant volcanic rock, a fine-grained, dark lava rich in iron and magnesium. It floors the ocean basins and erupts from fissures and shields wherever low-viscosity magma reaches the surface.

Rhyolite is the volcanic equivalent of granite, a pale, silica-rich rock that erupts from highly viscous magma. Its sluggish flow and high gas content favour the explosive eruptions that build domes and ash deposits.

Pahoehoe lava has a smooth, ropy surface formed where a fluid flow's skin is wrinkled by the still-moving liquid beneath. As the flow slows and its surface tears, it transforms into rubbly, clinkery aa.

Pillow lava forms when basaltic magma erupts underwater. The flow chills against the cold seawater into a glassy crust, and successive blobs squeeze out and stack into a pile of bulbous, pillow-shaped lobes.
Columnar jointing develops as a thick lava flow or sill cools and contracts. The contraction cracks the rock into a regular array of polygonal columns oriented perpendicular to the cooling surfaces.
Pumice is a frothy volcanic glass riddled with gas bubbles frozen in at the moment of eruption. So full of voids is the rock that some samples are light enough to float on water.
Obsidian is a volcanic glass formed when silica-rich lava cools too quickly for crystals to grow. Its smooth conchoidal fracture and sharp edges made it a prized material for ancient tools.
