An ignimbrite is the consolidated deposit of a pyroclastic flow, a sheet of ash and pumice laid down by a hot, ground-hugging avalanche. Where the deposit is hot enough, the glass shards fuse, or weld, into a dense rock.

Volcanic ash consists of fragments smaller than two millimetres, blasted out when escaping gas shatters the magma. Carried by the wind, the ash settles over wide areas to form layers useful for dating and correlation.
Tuff is a rock composed of compacted volcanic ash and lapilli. Its variety records the eruption that produced it, from quietly settled airfall ash to the welded deposits of violent pyroclastic flows.

Sedimentary rocks are grouped by origin into clastic, chemical, and biochemical types. Clastic rocks are built from broken fragments, chemical rocks precipitate from solution, and biochemical rocks are assembled by organisms.

Clastic sedimentary rocks are classified chiefly by grain size. Conglomerate is built of gravel-sized clasts, sandstone of sand, and shale of clay-sized particles too fine to see without magnification.
Sandstone is described by its composition as well as its texture. A quartz arenite is nearly pure quartz, an arkose is rich in feldspar, and a lithic sandstone contains abundant rock fragments.

Limestone is a carbonate rock formed largely from the calcareous remains of organisms. Its varieties include shelly coquina, fine-grained micrite, and the bioclastic accumulations of reefs and shoals.

Maturity describes how far a clastic sediment has progressed toward a stable, well-sorted, quartz-rich endpoint. A mature sandstone has been thoroughly worked, losing its unstable grains and acquiring rounded, well-sorted quartz.

Diagenesis encompasses the physical and chemical changes that turn loose sediment into solid rock. Compaction expels pore water and cementation precipitates mineral binder, lithifying the deposit as it is buried.

Dolostone forms when calcium in a limestone is partly replaced by magnesium, producing the mineral dolomite. The conversion commonly occurs after deposition, as magnesium-bearing fluids percolate through the carbonate.

Chert is a hard, microcrystalline silica rock that forms either by the accumulation of siliceous organisms or by the chemical replacement of carbonate. It occurs as bedded deposits and as nodules within limestone.
Sorting describes the uniformity of grain size in a clastic rock. A well-sorted sandstone, with grains of nearly equal size, records prolonged reworking by wind or waves before final deposition.

Rounding measures how far the sharp corners of a grain have been worn away during transport. Well-rounded grains have travelled far or been abraded long, while angular grains have moved only a short distance.

Geological hazards are natural processes that endanger life and property. Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides, floods, and ground subsidence each pose distinct threats that geologists work to anticipate and mitigate.

Land subsidence can follow the withdrawal of groundwater or hydrocarbons from beneath the surface. As the fluid pressure supporting the pore space drops, the sediment compacts and the ground sinks, sometimes by metres.
Expansive soils rich in swelling clay damage buildings as they take up and lose water. The seasonal heave and shrinkage cracks foundations, distorts pavements, and ruptures buried pipes.

Volcanic hazard maps delineate the zones threatened by lava flows, pyroclastic currents, ash fall, and lahars. They are built from the deposits of past eruptions, which record how far each process has previously reached.

A debris avalanche can be triggered by the collapse of an unstable volcanic edifice. The failed flank descends at high speed, carrying enormous blocks and leaving a hummocky deposit far from the volcano.

Sinkhole collapse is a hazard in karst terrain, where the dissolution of carbonate bedrock leaves cavities at depth. The sudden failure of an overlying soil arch can swallow structures without warning.

Coastal erosion threatens cliff-top development as waves undercut and remove the supporting rock. The rate of retreat depends on rock strength, wave energy, and the supply of protective beach sediment.

Radon is a radioactive gas released by the decay of uranium in certain rocks and soils. It can seep into buildings and accumulate to harmful concentrations, particularly above granites and uranium-rich shales.
Tsunami inundation maps forecast how far a wave might reach inland and how high it might rise. Modelled from plausible earthquake sources, they guide evacuation planning along vulnerable coasts.

Hazard assessment combines the likelihood of a damaging event with the exposure and vulnerability of the population. The product is the risk, the quantity that planners seek to reduce through siting, design, and warning.

An orogeny is a mountain-building episode driven by the collision and deformation of crustal blocks. Convergence thickens the crust, raises it into peaks, and metamorphoses its rocks in the heat of the deep interior.

Continental collision builds the highest mountains, as in the Himalaya, where two buoyant landmasses meet. Neither plate can readily subduct, so the crust crumples, stacks along thrusts, and is driven to great elevation.
A fold-and-thrust belt forms on the flank of a growing mountain range as the crust is shortened. Stacked thrust sheets and folds transport rock toward the foreland, away from the core of the orogen.

A foreland basin subsides under the weight of an advancing mountain belt. The thickening orogen flexes the adjacent crust downward, creating a trough that fills with sediment shed from the rising peaks.

Terrane accretion builds continents by welding fragments of crust onto their margins. Island arcs, plateaus, and slivers of ocean floor are scraped off a subducting plate and sutured to the overriding continent.

An ophiolite is a slice of oceanic crust and upper mantle thrust onto a continent during collision. Its layered sequence of pillow basalt, sheeted dykes, gabbro, and peridotite preserves a cross-section of a vanished ocean floor.

A suture zone marks the line along which two continents joined when the ocean between them closed. It is recognised by deformed deep-sea rocks, ophiolite fragments, and high-pressure metamorphic belts.

Isostasy governs the elevation of a mountain range, which floats on the denser mantle like an iceberg. A deep root of light crustal rock balances the towering peaks and adjusts as erosion strips the mountains down.

Orogenic collapse occurs when a thickened, over-steepened mountain belt spreads under its own weight. The crust extends, normal faults drop the high terrain, and the orogen relaxes toward a lower, broader profile.

Exhumation brings deeply buried metamorphic rocks back toward the surface during and after an orogeny. The combined effects of erosion and tectonic unroofing expose, in mountain cores, rocks once deep in the crust.

Diagenesis spans all the changes a sediment undergoes after deposition and before metamorphism. It begins at the sediment-water interface and continues through burial, transforming a loose deposit into a coherent rock.

Compaction reduces the volume of a sediment as the weight of overlying material squeezes the grains together. Pore water is expelled, the grains rearrange and interpenetrate, and porosity declines steadily with depth.

Cementation binds the grains of a sediment together as minerals precipitate from pore fluids in the void spaces. Quartz, calcite, and clay are common cements, and their growth lithifies the deposit while reducing its porosity.

Pressure solution dissolves rock at grain contacts where the stress is concentrated. The dissolved material migrates to lower-stress sites and reprecipitates, and the cumulative loss is recorded by jagged stylolite seams.
Dissolution during diagenesis can create as well as destroy porosity. The removal of unstable grains and earlier cements by aggressive pore fluids opens secondary porosity that may host hydrocarbons.

Recrystallisation rearranges the crystals of a rock without changing its bulk composition. A fine-grained limestone may coarsen into a mosaic of interlocking calcite crystals as it is buried and warmed.

Replacement substitutes one mineral for another while preserving the original texture. The conversion of limestone to dolostone and the silicification of wood are familiar examples of diagenetic replacement.
Concretions are localised, hard masses formed where cement precipitates around a nucleus within a sediment. They grow before the host is fully compacted and often enclose a fossil at their centre.
The diagenetic environment is divided by the chemistry of the pore water. The marine, meteoric, and deep burial realms each impose a characteristic suite of cements and alterations on the sediment.

Stylolites are irregular, suture-like seams concentrated with insoluble residue, marking surfaces of pressure solution. The amplitude of their teeth gives a rough measure of the rock dissolved away along the seam.
A joint is a fracture in rock along which no appreciable movement has occurred. Joints open the rock to weathering and fluid flow, and their orientation records the stresses the rock has experienced.

Joints commonly occur in sets of parallel fractures, and two or more intersecting sets form a joint system. The geometry of the system divides the rock into blocks and strongly influences how it erodes.

Sheet jointing develops parallel to a rock surface as erosion removes the overlying load. The unloaded rock expands and splits into curved sheets, a process that shapes the smooth domes of exposed granite.

Columnar joints form polygonal columns in cooling lava and shallow intrusions. The contraction of the cooling rock concentrates tensile stress at regularly spaced points, which propagate inward as the fractures grow.

Exfoliation joints curve concentrically around a rock mass, peeling it like an onion. They are an expression of the rock's adjustment to the release of confining pressure as the surface is lowered by erosion.

Tensile joints open perpendicular to the direction of least stress, and their surfaces preserve plumose markings. These delicate, feather-like patterns record the direction in which the fracture propagated.

Fracture density and connectivity govern the permeability of otherwise tight rock. In crystalline aquifers and tight reservoirs, the network of joints provides the only effective pathways for fluid to move.

Lineaments are long, straight topographic features visible on imagery, often the surface trace of deep fractures or faults. Mapping them reveals structural grain that may not be evident from the ground.

Joint spacing tends to scale with bed thickness, so thin beds are typically more closely jointed than thick ones. This relationship reflects how stress is transferred and relieved within layered rock.
Frost shattering exploits existing joints, prising the rock apart as water freezes within the fractures. Over time the widening joints reduce a jointed outcrop to a field of angular blocks.

Cross-bedding is a set of inclined laminae deposited on the advancing face of a migrating ripple or dune. The dip direction of the foresets records the current that built the bedform, making cross-beds a reliable palaeocurrent indicator.

Graded bedding shows a systematic change in grain size through a bed, typically coarse at the base and fining upward. It records deposition from a waning current, as the largest particles settle first and finer ones follow.

Ripple marks are small ridges sculpted on a sediment surface by moving water or wind. Symmetrical ripples indicate the back-and-forth motion of waves, while asymmetrical ones record a current flowing in one direction.
Mud cracks form as a fine-grained sediment dries and shrinks, splitting into a polygonal network of fissures. Their presence proves that the deposit was exposed to the air and allowed to desiccate.
Flute casts are scour marks on the base of a sandstone bed, moulded into the underlying mud by a turbulent current. Their flared, asymmetric shape points to the direction in which the current flowed.
Graded rhythmite couplets of sand and mud record episodic deposition, each pair laid down by a single event. The Bouma sequence formalises the internal divisions of an ideal turbidite bed.

Load casts are bulbous protrusions on the base of a sand bed that has sunk into soft mud beneath. They form while the sediment is still water-saturated, as the denser sand founders into the less dense layer below.

Hummocky cross-stratification consists of gently curving, dome-and-swale laminae produced by powerful storm waves. It records sedimentation on a shelf agitated by combined oscillatory and unidirectional flow.

Convolute lamination is a contorted, crumpled bedding produced by the deformation of soft sediment. The folding occurs before lithification, while the layers are still able to flow and slide over one another.

Geopetal structures record the original up direction in a rock. A partly sediment-filled cavity, with internal sediment below and a crystalline roof above, acts as a fossil spirit level showing which way was up.

When an igneous rock cools through a critical temperature, its magnetic minerals lock in the direction of the ambient field. This frozen magnetisation preserves a record of the Earth's field at the time of cooling.

The Earth's magnetic field has reversed polarity many times, and the record of these flips is written into the rocks. The pattern of normal and reversed intervals forms a magnetostratigraphic timescale used for correlation.

The inclination of the remanent magnetisation in a rock records the magnetic latitude at which it formed. Shallow inclinations indicate origin near the equator and steep ones near the poles, tracing a continent's drift.

Apparent polar wander paths plot the changing position of the magnetic pole as recorded by a continent's rocks. Because the pole is fixed, the path actually traces the wandering of the continent itself.

Symmetrical magnetic stripes flanking a mid-ocean ridge record seafloor spreading. Each band of crust freezes in the field's polarity as it forms, so the stripes archive the history of reversals as the plates move apart.
Detrital remanent magnetisation forms in sediment as magnetic grains settle and align with the field before burial. The resulting record allows the dating and correlation of sedimentary successions.

The Curie temperature is the threshold below which a mineral can retain a permanent magnetisation. Magnetite and hematite, the principal magnetic carriers in rocks, lock in the field as they cool past this point.

Reconstructing the breakup of a supercontinent relies on matching the paleomagnetic records of the now-separated fragments. Where their pole paths coincide for an interval, the pieces were joined during that time.
Magnetic anomalies measured at the surface betray buried bodies of strongly magnetic rock. The pattern of highs and lows guides the search for iron ore and maps concealed igneous intrusions.

A geomagnetic excursion is a brief, large departure of the field direction that stops short of a full reversal. Such events, recorded in rapidly deposited sediment, provide sharp time markers for correlation.
A pluton is a large body of igneous rock that crystallised slowly at depth. Its coarse, interlocking crystals reflect the unhurried cooling that allowed each mineral grain ample time to grow.

A batholith is an immense composite mass of intrusive rock, exposed over hundreds of square kilometres after deep erosion. It is assembled from many separate pulses of magma emplaced over millions of years.

A dyke is a sheet-like intrusion that cuts discordantly across the layering of the host rock. Dykes fill fractures opened by the magma's own pressure and commonly occur in radiating or parallel swarms.
A sill is a tabular intrusion injected parallel to the layering of the surrounding rock. It exploits a plane of weakness, such as a bedding surface, and prises the strata apart as the magma spreads.
A laccolith is a concordant intrusion that has domed the overlying rock upward. The magma ponds along a horizon and inflates into a lens, arching the strata above into a blister-like uplift.
A xenolith is a fragment of foreign rock enclosed within an igneous body. Torn from the wallrock or carried up from depth, xenoliths offer samples of rock otherwise inaccessible at the surface.
A chilled margin is the fine-grained selvage at the edge of an intrusion, where the magma cooled rapidly against the colder country rock. The grain size coarsens inward as the cooling rate slowed.
Stoping is a mechanism of magma emplacement in which the rising melt fractures and engulfs blocks of the roof. The dislodged fragments founder into the chamber, allowing the magma to ascend.

A contact aureole is the zone of altered rock around an intrusion, baked by the heat of the cooling magma. Its width and the metamorphic grade within it record the temperature and size of the intrusive body.

A volcanic neck is the solidified conduit of an extinct volcano, left standing in relief after the softer surrounding cone has been stripped away by erosion. It marks the central plumbing of the former vent.

The Antarctic Ice Sheet conceals an entire continent of bedrock, parts of which lie far below sea level. Radar surveys flown across the ice reveal buried mountain ranges, subglacial lakes, and deep trenches.

Ice cores drilled through polar ice sheets recover a continuous archive of past climate. Trapped air bubbles preserve samples of the ancient atmosphere, and the layered ice records hundreds of thousands of years of snowfall.
Permafrost is ground that remains frozen for at least two consecutive years. It underlies vast tracts of the high latitudes and locks immense quantities of carbon within its frozen organic matter.

Ice-wedge polygons pattern the surface of permafrost terrain. Repeated thermal contraction cracks the frozen ground, the cracks fill with ice, and over time a tessellated network of wedges divides the land into polygons.

Periglacial processes shape landscapes near, but not beneath, glacial ice. Frost heave, the sorting of stones into patterned ground, and the slow flow of thawed soil all bear the imprint of intense freezing and thawing.

Pingos are ice-cored mounds that rise from the floors of permafrost lowlands. They grow as water freezes beneath the surface and the expanding lens of ice heaves the overlying soil into a conspicuous hill.

The Transantarctic Mountains expose a long succession of sedimentary and igneous rock, including the coal-bearing strata that preserve fossils of ancient temperate forests. They record a time before the continent was glaciated.

Subglacial lakes lie sealed beneath kilometres of Antarctic ice, kept liquid by geothermal heat and the insulating ice above. The largest, Lake Vostok, has been isolated from the atmosphere for millions of years.
Glacial isostatic adjustment continues across formerly glaciated polar regions long after the ice has thinned. The crust slowly rebounds upward as the mantle flows back beneath the unloaded land.

Erratic boulders scattered across the polar landscape, and striated bedrock pavements, record the former extent of the ice. They mark how much further the ice sheets reached during past glacial maxima.

Caves form chiefly by the dissolution of soluble rock, as slightly acidic groundwater enlarges fractures into passages. Over long intervals the conduits coalesce into the branching systems explored by speleologists.

The level of a cave passage often records a former position of the water table. A multi-storey cave, with passages stacked at several heights, traces the stepwise lowering of the regional groundwater level.
Flowstone forms where a film of mineral-charged water spreads across a cave wall or floor. As the water loses carbon dioxide and deposits carbonate, it builds smooth, draped sheets of calcite.
Cave pearls form where dripping water keeps small grains in constant motion within a shallow pool. Each grain accretes concentric layers of calcite, growing into a polished, spherical pearl.

Lava tubes are caves formed within a flowing basaltic lava. The surface of the flow crusts over and solidifies while the molten interior drains away, leaving a hollow tunnel beneath the hardened roof.

A doline, or sinkhole, is the surface expression of underground dissolution. Solution dolines develop slowly as the rock dissolves, while collapse dolines form abruptly when the roof of a cavity gives way.
Cave deposits preserve a sensitive record of past climate. The growth rate and chemistry of stalagmites respond to rainfall and temperature, yielding precisely dated archives of environmental change.

Helictites are speleothems that twist and curl in defiance of gravity. They grow as water seeps through tiny central canals, and surface tension, rather than the pull of gravity, guides their erratic course.
Cave breakdown is the collapse of blocks from the ceiling and walls of a passage. The accumulated rubble records the gradual enlargement of the void as the cave matures and its roof becomes unstable.

Phreatic passages, dissolved below the water table, have smooth, rounded, tube-like cross-sections. Vadose passages, cut by free-flowing streams above the water table, are instead tall, narrow canyons.

Deserts are regions of sparse precipitation where physical weathering and wind dominate the shaping of the land. The scant vegetation leaves the bedrock and sediment exposed to the full force of these processes.
A playa is the flat floor of a desert basin that floods briefly after rare rains and then dries out. The evaporating water leaves a crust of salt and fine clay across the basin's lowest ground.
Desert pavement is a tightly packed surface mosaic of stones left behind as wind removes the finer material. The interlocking clasts armour the ground and protect it from further deflation.

Yardangs are streamlined ridges carved from soft rock by the abrasive action of wind-driven sand. Aligned with the prevailing wind, they resemble the inverted hulls of ships marching across the desert.
An inselberg is an isolated, steep-sided hill rising abruptly from a desert plain. It is a resistant remnant left standing as the surrounding, weaker rock is worn down around it.

Sand dunes take a variety of forms governed by sand supply and wind regime. Crescentic barchans migrate where sand is scarce, linear seif dunes run parallel to the wind, and star dunes build where winds blow from many directions.
Desert varnish is a thin, dark coating of clay and manganese and iron oxides on exposed rock surfaces. It accumulates over thousands of years and slowly darkens stones long left undisturbed.
A bajada is a continuous apron of sediment formed where adjacent alluvial fans, built at the mouths of mountain canyons, grow until they merge along the base of the range.
Ventifacts are stones whose faces have been ground flat and polished by wind-blown sand. Where the wind shifts direction, a stone may acquire several faceted surfaces meeting in sharp edges.
Wadis are the normally dry channels of desert streams. They carry water only during infrequent storms, when flash floods sweep down them, briefly transporting large volumes of sediment.

A plateau is an extensive area of elevated, relatively flat land bounded by steep slopes. Where horizontal strata are uplifted as a block, rivers dissect the surface but the flat-lying caprock keeps the summits level.
An escarpment is a long cliff or steep slope that separates two more gently inclined surfaces. It commonly marks the eroded edge of a resistant rock unit retreating across the landscape.
A cuesta is an asymmetric ridge formed on gently dipping strata. Its steep scarp face cuts across the beds, while its gentle dip slope follows the inclination of the resistant layer.
A mesa is a flat-topped, steep-sided upland capped by a resistant layer. It is an erosional remnant of a once more extensive plateau, isolated as the surrounding rock has been stripped away.
A butte is a small, isolated hill with steep sides and a narrow summit. It represents an advanced stage in the erosion of a mesa, reduced as its protective caprock is progressively consumed.
Scarp retreat is the slow backwearing of an escarpment as the cliff face is undermined and collapses. The hard caprock is sapped from below, and the freed blocks tumble to the slope at its foot.
Canyon incision occurs where an uplifted plateau is cut by a vigorous river. The stream entrenches itself in step with the uplift, carving a deep gorge through the flat-lying strata.

Differential erosion of layered rock produces a stepped topography of cliffs and benches. Resistant beds form vertical faces, while weaker beds erode into slopes, sculpting the staircase profile of a dissected plateau.
A structural bench is a flat shelf on a hillside formed where a resistant bed crops out. The hard layer holds up the bench while the softer rock above and below is etched back.

Pediments are gently sloping bedrock surfaces that flank a retreating mountain front. Thinly veneered with sediment, they grow wider as the mountain mass is worn back and the low-angle surface extends.

Mineral exploration searches systematically for economic concentrations of metals and other resources. It proceeds from broad regional surveys to focused drilling, narrowing the target at each stage of investigation.

Geochemical surveys sample soil, stream sediment, and water to detect the dispersed chemical halo around a concealed orebody. Anomalously high values guide explorers toward the hidden source of the metals.

Geophysical methods sense buried structure by measuring physical contrasts in the rock. Gravity, magnetic, and electrical surveys reveal dense ore, magnetic minerals, and conductive sulphides without disturbing the ground.

Drilling provides direct samples of the rock at depth. Diamond drilling recovers a continuous cylindrical core, preserving the geology intact, while reverse-circulation drilling returns chips at a faster, cheaper rate.

An ore reserve is the part of a mineral deposit that can be extracted economically under current conditions. It is estimated from the grade and tonnage defined by closely spaced drilling and rigorous sampling.

Remote sensing detects mineralisation from afar by measuring how rocks reflect different wavelengths of light. Distinctive spectral signatures betray the alteration minerals that often surround a buried ore deposit.
A gossan is the rusty, iron-stained outcrop left where a sulphide orebody has weathered at the surface. Early prospectors recognised these leached caps as a telltale sign of valuable ore at depth.
Cut-off grade is the lowest concentration of metal that can be mined at a profit. Material above the cut-off is classified as ore, while material below it is left as waste.

Pathfinder elements are easily detected species that travel with a sought-after but elusive metal. Arsenic and antimony, for instance, often accompany gold and broaden the chemical target an explorer can detect.

Resource estimation interpolates grade between the points sampled by drilling. Geostatistical methods weight the surrounding data according to spatial structure, producing a model of the deposit and a measure of its uncertainty.

A delta builds where a river deposits its sediment load on entering a standing body of water. The deposit grows seaward as long as the river supplies sediment faster than waves and tides can remove it.

Distributary channels carry the river's flow across the delta plain, splitting and rejoining as they cross the low-gradient surface. Sediment dropped along their courses builds the framework of the delta.

A river-dominated delta, such as that of the Mississippi, develops a digitate, bird-foot shape. Where the river overwhelms marine reworking, the distributaries extend long, sediment-fringed fingers into the basin.
A wave-dominated delta is reshaped by the persistent attack of waves, which redistribute the river sediment along the shore. The result is a smooth, arcuate shoreline fringed with beach ridges.

A tide-dominated delta is dissected by strong tidal currents that mould the sediment into elongate, channel-parallel sandbars. The river mouth is funnel-shaped, and the bars are flushed by the daily ebb and flood.

Delta progradation builds a coarsening-upward succession as the river mouth advances. Fine prodelta mud is buried beneath the sandier deposits of the delta front, which in turn pass up into the delta plain.

A crevasse splay forms when a river breaches its levee during a flood and spreads a tongue of sand across the adjacent floodplain or delta plain. Repeated splays nourish the wetlands between the active channels.
Delta lobe switching occurs when a river abandons one course for a shorter, steeper path to the sea. The old lobe, deprived of sediment, subsides and is eroded while a new lobe builds elsewhere.

Deltas subside under the weight of their own accumulating sediment, and the loose deposits compact with burial. Where the combined sinking outpaces sediment supply, the delta surface is gradually drowned.

The Gilbert-type delta, built into a deep lake or fjord, displays a clear three-part structure. Steep foreset beds of coarse sediment are sandwiched between gently inclined topsets and fine, flat-lying bottomsets.

The principle of superposition holds that in an undisturbed succession of sedimentary rocks, each layer is younger than the one beneath it. This simple rule establishes the relative order of deposition.

The principle of original horizontality states that sediments are laid down in nearly flat layers. Strata now found tilted or folded must therefore have been deformed by some event after their deposition.
The principle of cross-cutting relationships holds that a feature which cuts across a rock must be younger than the rock it disrupts. A fault or an intrusion postdates the strata it transects.

An unconformity is a buried surface of erosion or non-deposition that represents a gap in the rock record. It marks an interval during which no sediment was preserved, or during which rock was stripped away.

An angular unconformity separates tilted older strata from flat-lying younger beds. It records a full episode of deposition, deformation, and erosion before sedimentation resumed on the truncated surface.
The principle of inclusions states that fragments enclosed within a rock are older than the rock that contains them. A pebble in a conglomerate or a xenolith in a granite predates its host.

The principle of faunal succession holds that fossil organisms appear, change, and disappear in a fixed and recognisable order. This predictable sequence allows rocks to be correlated and relatively dated by their fossils.
A disconformity is an erosional gap between parallel strata, with no tilting to betray the missing time. It is recognised by the erosion surface itself and by the fossils absent across the break.
A nonconformity separates younger sedimentary rock from older crystalline igneous or metamorphic rock below. It records the deep erosion of the basement before the sediments were laid across it.

Lateral continuity holds that sedimentary layers extend outward in all directions until they thin to nothing or meet a barrier. Strata of the same age on opposite sides of a valley were once a single continuous deposit.
